items.title: [Bug]: Reasoning models inherit chat-model stale-timeout defaults — broken-pipe on long-thinking models like Nemotron 3 Ultra, OpenAI o1/o3, Opus 4.x thinking

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Bug Description

Hermes's default stale-stream detector (`HERMES_STREAM_STALE_TIMEOUT` = 180s, `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2540`) and default non-stream stale detector (`HERMES_API_CALL_STALE_TIMEOUT` = 90s, `run_agent.py:1140-1156`) are calibrated for fast-responding chat models. Reasoning models — NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, OpenAI o1/o3, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.x thinking, DeepSeek R1, Qwen QwQ, xAI Grok reasoning variants — routinely exceed those windows during their thinking phase.

The codebase already has an auto-scaling mechanism for large contexts (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2548-2559` raises the stale timeout to 240s for 50k–100k token contexts and 300s for >100k token contexts) and explicit per-model timeout overrides in `tests/hermes_cli/test_timeouts.py` for Anthropic Opus (`claude-opus-4.6: timeout_seconds: 120`) and OpenAI-codex (`gpt-5.4: stale_timeout_seconds: 1800`). But there is **no equivalent for known reasoning models** — a user picking `nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b` or `deepseek-r1` or `o3-mini` inherits the 180s/90s defaults and trips the stale detector mid-think, surfacing as `BrokenPipeError` from the upstream proxy (NVIDIA NIM's 60-180s idle kill, OpenAI's worker idle timeout, Anthropic's stream idle timeout, etc.).

The result is exclusive-to-reasoning-model failures of the form `API call failed after 3 retries: [Errno 32] Broken pipe`. Same first-party reproduction at NVIDIA/NemoClaw#4846 (Nemotron 3 Ultra, 120s upstream idle kill, 31s TTFB). Industry-parallel: anthropics/claude-code#49619 (Opus 4.7 thinking), OpenAI Community #1254230 (o1/o3).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a reasoning model: any of `nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b`, `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b`, `deepseek/deepseek-r1`, `openai/o3-mini`, `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6` (thinking variant), `qwen/qwq-32b-preview`, `x-ai/grok-4-fast-reasoning`, or their OpenRouter-routed equivalents.
2. Send a prompt that triggers extended thinking (multi-minute first-token latency on these models is normal for non-trivial prompts).
3. Observe the stale-stream detector at `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2584-2588` killing the connection at 180s (`HERMES_STREAM_STALE_TIMEOUT` default) or the non-stream stale detector at `run_agent.py:1114-1156` killing at 90s (`HERMES_API_CALL_STALE_TIMEOUT` default).
4. User sees the same `API call failed after 3 retries: [Errno 32] Broken pipe` shape — error from the upstream proxy closing the socket, not from hermes's own logic.

The auto-scaling for large contexts at `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2553-2559` only fires when `approx_tokens > 50_000` (i.e. only for sessions that are already large). A fresh conversation with a reasoning model on a small context still hits the 180s ceiling.

## Expected Behavior

The stale-stream and non-stream stale detectors automatically scale up for known reasoning models when the user has not explicitly configured `providers.<id>.models.<model>.stale_timeout_seconds` (or `request_timeout_seconds` for the non-stream path). The scaling is a `max(...)` floor — never lowers an existing threshold and never overrides explicit user config.

## Actual Behavior

Reasoning-model users get the 180s/90s chat-model defaults and hit upstream-broken-pipe failures.

## Affected Component

- Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)
- Configuration (config.yaml, .env, hermes setup) — for the resolution path
- Other: `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py`, `run_agent.py`, `agent/agent_init.py`

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only) — but the gateway path inherits the same bug because the retry loop and stale detector are in shared `agent/` modules.

## Debug Report

N/A — manually reproducible from the cited file:line references. The default values are read from `env_float("HERMES_STREAM_STALE_TIMEOUT", 180.0)` at `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2540` and `env_float("HERMES_API_CALL_STALE_TIMEOUT", 90.0)` at `run_agent.py:1140-1156`. The auto-scaling for large contexts is at `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2553-2559` and `run_agent.py:1156-1170` (the latter is gated by context-size; the former is hardcoded to the configured `HERMES_STREAM_STALE_TIMEOUT` default for the no-large-context branch).

## Operating System

macOS 15.2 (also reproducible on Linux/Windows — bug is in pure-Python source, OS-independent)

## Python Version

3.11.9

## Hermes Version

`8f0a12ce0` (current `main`)

## Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

The relevant log lines from `agent.log` on a Nemotron 3 Ultra thinking-timeout failure:

```
WARNING Stream drop on attempt 1/3 — retrying. subagent_id=- depth=0 provider=nvidia base_url=https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1 error_type=APIConnectionError error=Error communicating with OpenAI: [Errno 32] Broken pipe chain=APIConnectionError(...) <- BrokenPipeError([Errno 32] Broken pipe) http_status=- bytes=0 chunks=0 elapsed=120.34s ttfb=- upstream=[cf-ray=... x-request-id=...]
WARNING Stream stale for 180s (threshold 180s) — no chunks received. model=nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b context=~12,000 tokens. Killing connection.
ERROR  API call failed after 3 retries. <summary> | provider=nvidia model=nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b msgs=24 tokens=~12,000
```

The `elapsed=120.34s` on the first drop is the smoking gun — upstream killed at 120s (NVIDIA NIM's idle window), well before hermes's 180s stale detector would have fired on a healthy reasoning-model stream.

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The codebase already has the right pattern, applied to two other reasoning-model contexts:

1. **Anthropic Opus per-model timeout fixture** — `tests/hermes_cli/test_timeouts.py:15-29` documents `claude-opus-4.6: timeout_seconds: 120` and `tests/hermes_cli/test_timeouts.py:46-60` documents `gpt-5.4: stale_timeout_seconds: 1800`. Both are explicit per-model overrides — they require the user to know about the knob and to write the config.

2. **Per-model reasoning-effort allowlist** — `agent/model_metadata.py:322-339` (`grok_supports_reasoning_effort`) uses substring matching (longest-first) on model slugs to identify models that accept `reasoning.effort`. The same pattern is the natural fit for identifying reasoning models that need extended timeouts — the substring must be available *before* the request is dispatched, and response-side signals (`reasoning_content`, `reasoning_details`) are unavailable at that point. Implicit reasoning models (Nemotron 3 Ultra, DeepSeek R1) don't accept explicit `enable_thinking` / `reasoning_effort` request keys, so request-side signals are incomplete.

The missing piece is a **per-reasoning-model stale-timeout floor** that lives between the existing default and the user-configurable per-model override — a sensible default for known reasoning models that helps users who don't know about the per-model override knob, while never overriding explicit user config.

The cleanest implementation follows the existing `grok_supports_reasoning_effort` pattern at `agent/model_metadata.py:322-339`: a static substring-keyed floor map with longest-substring-first matching. Key design constraints (derived from cross-vendor review of an earlier draft of this proposal):

- **Trailing-hyphen keys.** `"o1-"` instead of `"o1"`, `"claude-opus-"` instead of `"claude-opus"`, etc. Avoids false positives on community derivatives and future model names. Bare `"o1"` would match `"olmo-1"` or hypothetical `"llama-4-70b-o1"`; `"o1-"` does not (because olmo-1 has no hyphen after "1").
- **Longest-substring-first match.** Same algorithm as `grok_supports_reasoning_effort` at line 342-345. Stable on model-prefix routing (`openai/o1-preview` still matches `"o1-"`).
- **`max(...)` floor, never replaces.** The floor only raises the existing default — never lowers it. Explicit user config (`providers.<id>.models.<model>.stale_timeout_seconds` set in config.yaml) always wins.
- **No effect on non-reasoning models.** Models not in the allowlist see zero behavior change.

## Proposed Fix (optional)

Add a new module `agent/reasoning_timeouts.py`:

```python
# Per-model stale-timeout floor for known reasoning models.
#
# Reasoning models (those that emit extended thinking blocks before
# their first content token) routinely exceed Hermes's default chat-
# model stale detectors (180s stream, 90s non-stream). Without a
# floor, the stale detector kills the connection mid-think, surfacing
# as upstream BrokenPipeError / RemoteProtocolError on the next read.
#
# This module provides a substring-keyed floor that the existing
# stale-detector scaling blocks at:
#   - agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2548-2559 (stream)
#   - run_agent.py:1114-1170 (non-stream)
# consult via get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor() and apply as
# max(default, floor). Never overrides explicit per-model
# providers.<id>.models.<model>.stale_timeout_seconds config.
#
# Substring keys use a trailing hyphen (e.g. 'o1-' not 'o1') to avoid
# matching community derivatives with overlapping names ('olmo-1',
# 'llama-4-70b-o1', 'claude-opus-other'). Longest substring wins so
# specific keys ('o3-mini-') beat general ones ('o3-').

from __future__ import annotations

# (key_substring, floor_seconds). Order is irrelevant — resolver does
# longest-substring-first match.
_REASONING_STALE_TIMEOUT_FLOORS: tuple[tuple[str, int], ...] = (
    # NVIDIA Nemotron — reasoning models behind hosted NIM with documented
    # 60-180s upstream idle kill (NVIDIA/NemoClaw#4846: 120s measured).
    ("nemotron-3-ultra-", 600),
    ("nemotron-3-super-", 600),
    ("nemotron-3-nano-",  300),
    # DeepSeek — R1 reasoning model on hosted NIM / DeepSeek direct.
    ("deepseek-r1",       600),
    ("deepseek-reasoner", 600),
    # Qwen — QwQ reasoning + Qwen3 thinking variants.
    ("qwq-",              300),
    ("qwen3-",            180),
    # OpenAI o-series — known multi-minute TTFB.
    ("o1-",               600),
    ("o3-mini-",          300),
    ("o3-",               600),
    ("o4-mini-",          300),
    # Anthropic Claude 4.x thinking variants.
    ("claude-opus-",      240),
    ("claude-sonnet-4.5", 180),
    ("claude-sonnet-4.6", 180),
    # xAI Grok reasoning variants (must be explicit, bare 'grok' too broad).
    ("grok-4-fast-reasoning", 300),
    ("grok-4.20-reasoning",   300),
    ("grok-4-fast-non-reasoning", 180),
)


def get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(model: str | None) -> float | None:
    # Return the stale-timeout floor (seconds) for a known reasoning model.
    # Returns None if the model is not in the allowlist or the argument
    # is empty. Substring match is longest-first to allow specific
    # variants (o3-mini-) to beat general ones (o3-) on shared prefixes.
    # This is a FLOOR — callers must apply it as max(default, floor)
    # and only when no explicit user-configured per-model
    # stale_timeout_seconds exists.
    if not model:
        return None
    # Sort by key length descending so longer / more-specific keys win.
    sorted_keys = sorted(_REASONING_STALE_TIMEOUT_FLOORS, key=lambda kv: -len(kv[0]))
    model_lower = model.lower()
    for key, floor in sorted_keys:
        if key in model_lower:
            return float(floor)
    return None
```

Integration points (small surgical edits, no behavior change for non-reasoning models):

`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py` — extend the existing context-size scaling block at line 2548-2559:

```python
_est_tokens = estimate_request_context_tokens(api_kwargs)
if _est_tokens > 100_000:
    _stream_stale_timeout = max(_stream_stale_timeout_base, 300.0)
elif _est_tokens > 50_000:
    _stream_stale_timeout = max(_stream_stale_timeout_base, 240.0)
else:
    _stream_stale_timeout = _stream_stale_timeout_base

# NEW: floor for known reasoning models. Only applies when no explicit
# per-model user config exists (the get_provider_stale_timeout check
# at line 2536-2538 already handled that path). Never lowers existing
# value.
from agent.reasoning_timeouts import get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor
_reasoning_floor = get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(api_kwargs.get("model"))
if _reasoning_floor is not None:
    _stream_stale_timeout = max(_stream_stale_timeout, _reasoning_floor)
```

`run_agent.py` — extend `_resolved_api_call_stale_timeout_base` at line 1114-1140:

```python
cfg = get_provider_stale_timeout(self.provider, self.model)
if cfg is not None:
    return cfg, False

env_timeout = os.getenv("HERMES_API_CALL_STALE_TIMEOUT")
if env_timeout is not None:
    return float(env_timeout), False

# NEW: floor for known reasoning models.
from agent.reasoning_timeouts import get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor
_reasoning_floor = get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(self.model)
if _reasoning_floor is not None:
    return _reasoning_floor, False

return 90.0, True  # existing default
```

Test coverage (single parametrized test, per cross-vendor review of an earlier draft — adding a fixture per model is unnecessary maintenance burden):

```python
@pytest.mark.parametrize("model,expected", [
    ("nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b", 600.0),
    ("openai/o3-mini",                    300.0),
    ("anthropic/claude-opus-4-6",         240.0),
    ("deepseek/deepseek-r1",              600.0),
    ("gpt-4o",                            None),  # non-reasoning, no floor
    ("olmo-1",                            None),  # bare 'o1' would match this; 'o1-' does not
    ("x-ai/grok-4-fast-reasoning",        300.0),
    ("x-ai/grok-4-fast-non-reasoning",    180.0),
])
def test_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(model, expected):
    from agent.reasoning_timeouts import get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor
    assert get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(model) == expected
```

- #41898 — `[Bug]: Desktop app — assistant response flashes and disappears immediately (provider: NVIDIA NIM)` — adjacent symptom on the same provider.
- #19883 — `[Feature]: Native reasoning_effort support for NVIDIA NIM (integrate.api.nvidia.com)` — adjacent feature request.
- NVIDIA/NemoClaw#4846 — first-party reproduction of the exact failure mode on `nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b` (NVIDIA's own stack).

items.title: Auxiliary rate-limit fallback bypassed for explicit providers

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Bug

When an auxiliary task is configured with an **explicit** provider (e.g. `openai-codex` / `gpt-5.5`) and that provider returns a 429 rate-limit error, the fallback chain is **never triggered**. The agent silently fails instead of falling back to an alternative provider.

## Root cause

In `agent/auxiliary_client.py`, the `is_capacity_error` gate only includes payment errors and connection errors — not rate limits:

```python
is_capacity_error = _is_payment_error(first_err) or _is_connection_error(first_err)
```

Later, the fallback is gated by:

```python
if should_fallback and (is_auto or is_capacity_error):
```

So when `resolved_provider` is explicit (not `"auto"`) and the error is a 429 rate-limit, `should_fallback` is `True` but `is_capacity_error` is `False` → fallback is skipped entirely.

## Impact

All auxiliary tasks (`kanban_decomposer`, `vision`, `web_extract`, `approval`, `profile_describer`, `curator`, etc.) that use an explicit provider have **zero resilience** to rate limits. When the provider is rate-limited, these tasks fail silently, degrading the agent experience (e.g. Kanban decomposition falls back to the main agent doing it inline).

## Fix

Add `_is_rate_limit_error(first_err)` to `is_capacity_error`:

```python
is_capacity_error = (
    _is_payment_error(first_err)
    or _is_connection_error(first_err)
    or _is_rate_limit_error(first_err)
)
```

Rate limits are capacity errors — after retries are exhausted, the provider literally cannot serve the request. The fallback chain should kick in regardless of whether the provider was auto-detected or explicitly configured.

## Reproduction

1. Configure an auxiliary task with an explicit provider:
   ```yaml
   auxiliary:
     kanban_decomposer:
       provider: openai-codex
       model: gpt-5.5
   ```
2. Trigger enough requests to hit the rate limit
3. Observe: no fallback occurs, task fails
4. Expected: `fallback_chain` entries are tried in order

The recovery UI then tells the user to sign in from Settings, but Settings is inaccessible because Desktop has not booted.

Observed behavior:
- Desktop connects to the configured remote backend and logs: "Remote Hermes backend is ready".
- The cached remote backend can then fail liveness and drop the stale connection.
- Desktop repeatedly fails startup with: "Your remote gateway session has expired. Open Settings → Gateway and click 'Sign in' again".
- Other retries fail with: "Hermes backend did not become ready: Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 15000ms".
- Retry/Repair clears the latched failure, but the same remote backend flow can repeat and still does not provide a usable sign-in path.

Expected behavior:
- If a remote backend requires re-authentication, Desktop should show a usable sign-in/re-auth flow before startup completes.
- If Desktop supports token-configured remote mode, the WebSocket and API calls used during startup should accept the configured remote token consistently.
- The recovery screen should not instruct the user to open Settings when Settings cannot be opened.

Actual behavior:
- The backend can be reachable and reported ready, but Desktop remains blocked on the startup recovery screen.
- The error messaging suggests a session/auth problem, but no actionable login UI is available from the failed boot state.
- Repair install does not resolve the issue because the failure appears to be remote auth/session compatibility, not a broken local install.

Technical notes:
This appears to be a mismatch between Desktop remote startup auth and the authenticated dashboard/backend auth layer.

In the failing setup, normal status/liveness checks could succeed while the Desktop startup path still failed. Allowing the configured legacy Desktop token for both the WebSocket startup path and authenticated API calls restored Desktop remote startup locally.

Suggested fix:
- Make Desktop remote mode and authenticated gateway mode use a single compatible auth contract.
- If basic/session auth is required, Desktop should present the login flow during remote boot failure.
- If token-based environment-variable remote mode is still supported, ensure both WebSocket and REST/API startup calls accept that token consistently.
- Improve the recovery screen so "session expired" does not point to Settings when Settings cannot be opened.

Prepared with assistance from Hermes Agent using GPT-5.5 Codex.

items.title: [Bug]: Reasoning models hit phantom context-overflow on thinking-timeout (Nemotron 3 Ultra, OpenAI o1/o3, Opus 4.x thinking) — silent compression on large sessions + misleading file-write guidance

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Bug Description

When a reasoning model (NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, OpenAI o1/o3, Anthropic Opus 4.x thinking, DeepSeek R1, Qwen QwQ, xAI Grok reasoning) hits a transport-layer error mid-thinking on a long session, the user sees one of two incorrect messages:

1. **`API call failed after 3 retries: [Errno 32] Broken pipe`** with no actionable guidance, OR
2. **The misleading "try `execute_code` with Python's `open()` for large files" advice** that fires for an unrelated bug class (large file-write stream drops).

Both are wrong for the thinking-timeout case. The actual root cause is that the upstream proxy idle-killed a long thinking stream (NVIDIA NIM ~120s — first-party reproduction at NVIDIA/NemoClaw#4846; OpenAI worker / Anthropic stream-idle similar), and the user needs actionable workarounds (raise `stale_timeout_seconds`, lower `reasoning_budget`, or switch to a smaller reasoning model).

The bug has two distinct layers that need separate fixes.

### Layer 1 — Classifier misclassification (load-bearing bug)

`agent/error_classifier.py:718-732` routes transport disconnects on large sessions to `FailoverReason.context_overflow, should_compress=True`. For reasoning models on a long session, this is wrong: it routes the user into the context-compression branch (`agent/conversation_loop.py:3037-3149`), which calls `_compress_context()` and eventually returns "Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached" — silently deleting conversation history on a **phantom** context-length error.

The classifier can't tell apart "real context overflow" from "upstream proxy idle-killed a long thinking stream" — both present as a transport-layer disconnect on a large session. For reasoning models specifically, the upstream-killed case is far more common than real overflow.

### Layer 2 — Wrong user-facing guidance

When the classifier routes correctly to `timeout` (small-session case) or after Layer 1 is fixed (large-session case), the existing `_is_stream_drop` substring check at `agent/conversation_loop.py:3464-3486` triggers the misleading "try `execute_code` with Python's `open()` for large files" message at lines 3504-3512. That advice is for the unrelated large-file-write stream-drop case and is actively wrong for the thinking-timeout case (the user did not write a file; the model was thinking).

The fix is a new `_is_thinking_timeout` branch that fires ONLY when the model is in the reasoning allowlist AND the failure is transport-layer AND no real content was streamed. It should append reasoning-specific guidance instead of the file-write guidance.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a reasoning model: `nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b`, `openai/o3-mini`, `anthropic/claude-opus-4-6`, `deepseek/deepseek-r1`, etc.
2. Build a session to >120k tokens or >200 messages (forces the "large session" branch in the classifier).
3. Send a prompt that triggers extended thinking (multi-minute first-token latency on reasoning models is normal for non-trivial prompts).
4. The upstream proxy times out (NVIDIA NIM ~120s idle kill) and the socket closes.
5. Observe:
   - **Without this fix:** `agent.log` shows the classifier routing to `context_overflow`, `_compress_context()` is called 3 times, eventually the user sees "Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached" — conversation history is silently compressed/dropped on a phantom overflow.
   - **With the fix:** classifier routes to `timeout`, retry path is followed, on terminal failure the user sees actionable guidance with three workarounds in priority order.

## Expected Behavior

When a reasoning model's thinking phase exceeds the upstream proxy's idle timeout on a long session:

1. The classifier should classify the error as `FailoverReason.timeout` (NOT `context_overflow`).
2. The compression branch should NOT fire — no phantom overflow.
3. The user should see reasoning-specific guidance with three actionable workarounds, not the misleading file-write advice.

## Actual Behavior

Without this fix:

1. Classifier routes to `context_overflow` on large sessions regardless of model family.
2. Compression branch fires, conversation history is silently truncated.
3. User sees either `Context length exceeded` (if compression exhausts) or the misleading "try `execute_code` with Python's `open()` for large files" advice (if compression somehow succeeds on a non-context issue).

## Affected Component

- Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)
- Other: `agent/error_classifier.py`, `agent/conversation_loop.py`

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only) — but the gateway path inherits the same bug because the retry loop and classifier are in shared `agent/` modules.

## Debug Report

N/A — manually reproducible in code paths cited above. The behavior is deterministic from the source: `agent/error_classifier.py:718-732` is a static rule; `agent/conversation_loop.py:3464-3512` is a static substring check.

## Operating System

macOS 15.2 (also reproducible on Linux/Windows — bug is in pure-Python source, OS-independent)

## Python Version

3.11.9

## Hermes Version

`411faf08b` (current `main`)

## Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

The relevant log lines from `agent.log` on a Nemotron 3 Ultra thinking-timeout failure on a long session:

```
ERROR  agent.error_classifier:error_classifier.py:727 Disconnect with large session → routing to context_overflow for compression
WARN   agent.conversation_loop:conversation_loop.py:3150 🗜️ Context too large (~130,000 tokens) — compressing (1/3)...
WARN   agent.conversation_loop:conversation_loop.py:3150 🗜️ Context too large (~130,000 tokens) — compressing (2/3)...
WARN   agent.conversation_loop:conversation_loop.py:3150 🗜️ Context too large (~130,000 tokens) — compressing (3/3)...
ERROR  agent.conversation_loop:conversation_loop.py:3145 Context length exceeded: max compression attempts (3) reached.
```

Note: the user did not actually exceed context length. The proxy killed the connection mid-think. The classifier routed the user into the compression branch on a phantom overflow.

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)

### Layer 1 root cause

`agent/error_classifier.py:718-732` runs the disconnect+large-session check before any reasoning-model awareness. The intent of the rule (per its comment at line 712-716) is "a disconnect on a large session is more likely context overflow than a transient transport hiccup." That heuristic is correct for chat models (gpt-4o, claude-3-5-sonnet) where the proxy doesn't idle-kill during prefill or generation. But for reasoning models, the upstream proxy **does** routinely idle-kill during multi-minute thinking phases — the heuristic inverts.

The classifier's `model` parameter is already in scope (the function signature has it at line 2245 of conversation_loop.py). The classifier just doesn't consult any reasoning-model allowlist. The fix is to consult `agent/reasoning_timeouts.get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(model)` BEFORE the `is_large` check; if the model is a known reasoning model, route to `timeout` (not `context_overflow`).

### Layer 2 root cause

`agent/conversation_loop.py:3504-3512` has a single `_is_stream_drop` substring check that fires for any "connection lost" / "connection reset" / etc. message. There's no branch for the thinking-timeout case. The fix is a new `_is_thinking_timeout` branch that fires when (a) model is in the reasoning allowlist, (b) failure is transport-layer, (c) `classified.reason == timeout`, (d) message contains a transport-kill substring.

## Proposed Fix (optional)

### Layer 1 — Classifier override (1 file, ~15 lines)

Add a reasoning-model override to `classify_api_error` in `agent/error_classifier.py`, BEFORE the `is_large` check at line 726:

```python
is_disconnect = any(p in error_msg for p in _SERVER_DISCONNECT_PATTERNS)
if is_disconnect and not status_code:
    # Reasoning-model override: a transport disconnect on a reasoning
    # model is much more likely the upstream proxy idle-killing a
    # long thinking stream than a true context overflow — even on
    # large sessions.  Without this, large-session reasoning-model
    # disconnects route to the compression branch and silently delete
    # conversation history on a phantom context-length error.
    from agent.reasoning_timeouts import get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor
    if get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(model) is not None:
        return _result(FailoverReason.timeout, retryable=True)
    is_large = approx_tokens > context_length * 0.6 or (
        context_length <= 256000 and (approx_tokens > 120000 or num_messages > 200)
    )
    if is_large:
        return _result(
            FailoverReason.context_overflow,
            retryable=True,
            should_compress=True,
        )
    return _result(FailoverReason.timeout, retryable=True)
```

### Layer 2 — Thinking-timeout detection + guidance (2 files, ~75 lines + a new module)

**New module `agent/thinking_timeout_guidance.py`:**

```python
def is_thinking_timeout(classified, model, error_msg) -> bool:
    # True iff reasoning model + transport-layer failure + timeout reason.
    from agent.reasoning_timeouts import get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor
    if getattr(getattr(classified, "reason", None), "value", None) != "timeout":
        return False
    if get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor(model) is None:
        return False
    return any(p in (error_msg or "").lower() for p in (
        "broken pipe", "errno 32", "remote protocol",
        "connection reset", "connection lost",
        "peer closed", "server disconnected",
    ))


def build_thinking_timeout_guidance(provider, model, model_label=None) -> str:
    # Return user-facing guidance string for thinking-timeout failures.
    label = model_label or model
    return (
        "\n\nThe model's thinking phase exceeded the upstream proxy's "
        f"idle timeout before the first content token arrived. This is a "
        f"known issue with reasoning models (like {label}) behind cloud "
        "gateways (NVIDIA NIM, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek). Workarounds "
        "in priority order:\n"
        f"1. Set `providers.{provider}.models.{model}.stale_timeout_seconds: 900` "
        "in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` to extend the per-call timeout. "
        "(Hermes's built-in floor is 600s for known reasoning models — "
        "if you still see this after raising, the upstream cap is even "
        "shorter.)\n"
        "2. Lower `reasoning_budget` or set `reasoning_effort: medium` on this "
        "model if the provider supports it.\n"
        "3. Use a smaller / faster reasoning model if the task doesn't "
        "require deep thinking."
    )
```

**Integration into `agent/conversation_loop.py` at lines 3486 and 3504:**

```python
# At line 3486 (after the existing `_is_stream_drop` vprint block):
from agent.thinking_timeout_guidance import is_thinking_timeout
_is_thinking_timeout = is_thinking_timeout(classified, _model, error_msg)
if _is_thinking_timeout:
    agent._vprint(...)  # 5 vprint calls with the three workarounds

# At line 3504 (replace the `_is_stream_drop` if with `if/elif`):
if _is_thinking_timeout:
    from agent.thinking_timeout_guidance import build_thinking_timeout_guidance
    _final_response += build_thinking_timeout_guidance(
        provider=_provider, model=_model,
    )
elif _is_stream_drop:
    _final_response += (  # unchanged existing guidance
        "\n\nThe provider's stream connection keeps "
        ...
    )
```

The new guidance takes precedence (`if/elif`) so a reasoning-model user with a transport-kill message sees the actionable reasoning-specific advice, not the misleading file-write advice.

## Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

## Related issues

- #52217 — Reasoning-model stale-timeout floor (Fixes the upstream stale-timeout defaults; this issue's Layer 1 override reuses the same `agent/reasoning_timeouts.get_reasoning_stale_timeout_floor` allowlist).
- #52216 — BrokenPipeError pool-recovery (Fixes the recovery-gate inconsistency; this issue's Layer 2 guidance fires on the now-correctly-routed timeout failures).
- NVIDIA/NemoClaw#4846 — first-party reproduction of `Broken pipe (os error 32)` on `nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b` after 120s upstream idle kill.
- anthropics/claude-code#49619 — industry-parallel: same broken-pipe-on-reasoning-model pattern on Anthropic Opus 4.7 thinking.
- OpenAI Community #1254230 — same pattern on OpenAI o1/o3.

## Dependency note for maintainers

The PR for this issue will include `agent/reasoning_timeouts.py` (the reasoning-model allowlist module) because PR #52217's allowlist is the load-bearing dependency for the Layer 1 override. After PR #52217 lands on `main`, the duplicate `agent/reasoning_timeouts.py` in this PR's diff should be rebased away — the maintainer can choose whichever PR lands first; the other rebase is mechanical (drop the duplicate file).

items.title: Deleted profile respawns indefinitely, accumulating zombie backend processes

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
**Environment**
- macOS (Apple Silicon, M2)
- Hermes Desktop (Electron)
- Hermes Agent backend (Python)

**Steps to Reproduce**
1. Create a non-default profile (e.g. `omlx`) via the Desktop UI
2. Delete the profile via the Desktop UI or `hermes profile delete omlx --yes`
3. Restart the Desktop

**Expected Behavior**
Profile is permanently deleted and does not reappear.

**Actual Behavior**
The deleted profile reappears after every restart. Investigation revealed:
- The Desktop spawns a new Python backend process (`hermes_cli.main --profile <name> dashboard`) every time it attempts to connect to the profile
- Old backend processes are never killed — PIDs accumulate across restarts (8+ zombie processes observed, dating back several days)
- Each new backend process recreates the profile directory on startup, causing `hermes profile list` to show the deleted profile again
- This creates an infinite loop: Desktop sees profile → spawns backend → backend recreates folder → Desktop sees profile again
- `hermes profile delete` successfully removes the folder and reports success, but the Desktop immediately respawns the backend which recreates the folder

**Root Cause (suspected)**
- Desktop does not track backend process PIDs for non-default profiles
- No cleanup of backend processes on profile deletion
- Backend dashboard command recreates the profile directory on startup if it does not exist
- Deletion is not propagated to the Desktop's process manager, leaving a dangling respawn loop

**Workaround**
```
pkill -f "hermes_cli.main --profile <name>"
hermes profile delete <name> --yes
```
Killing all backend processes for the profile *before* deleting it breaks the loop.

**Impact**
- Profile cannot be deleted through normal UI or CLI workflows
- Zombie Python processes accumulate indefinitely, consuming memory
- Users have no indication this is happening

items.title: Predefined Subagent Roles + Profile-backed Delegation + Orchestration Layer

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Summary

`delegate_task` already supports parallel batches, isolated context, leaf/orchestrator roles, and depth limits. What's missing is the orchestration layer that lets users **pre-define subagent roles** (model, toolsets, skills, system prompt preset), **pin them to profiles** for hard isolation, **guide the parent agent on when to delegate** (fixes #48217), and **coordinate multi-subagent workflows** (sequential, conflict resolution, quality gates) without hand-rolled glue logic.

This consolidates what is currently split across #7517, #41889, #46880, #35688, #5876, #28767 — each captures a slice; this is the integration.

---

## Problem

Every time I want "my architect to review this design", I write:

```python
delegate_task(
    goal="Review the attached architecture doc",
    context="""You are a senior architect. Use the plan skill.
    Output JSON: {decision, rationale, artifact}.
    Constraints: no implementation code, no external API.""",
    toolsets=["terminal", "file"],
    role="leaf",
)
```

Four failures:

1. **Identity is rebuilt every call.** Role prompt, tools, blocked tools, skill hints all live as a string in `context`. One paraphrase and the role silently changes.
2. **No memory across sessions.** Roles are re-authored from scratch each conversation.
3. **Parent agent has no delegation guidance.** #48217 documents this — agents do everything inline even when `delegate_task` would be cheaper. The tool gives no signal.
4. **No profile-backed delegation.** #41889 captures this — subagents inherit the parent's profile. If I have an `architect` profile with a different model and SOUL, I can't point `delegate_task` at it.
5. **Multi-subagent coordination is hand-rolled.** Architect → backend → qa on the same change? I write the orchestration in my own head — who goes first, what they pass, how conflicts resolve. None of that is expressible.

---

## Proposed (directional, not final)

**1. Role preset in config**

```yaml
agents:
  roles:
    architect:
      model: anthropic/claude-opus-4
      toolsets: [terminal, file]
      skills: [plan, spike, requesting-code-review]
      blocked_tools: [delegate_task, clarify, messaging]
      system_prompt_preset: |
        You are a senior architect. Review designs, not implementations.
        Output JSON: {decision, rationale, artifact}.
      profile: architect   # optional: pin to a profile for hard isolation
```

**2. Profile-backed delegation** (extends #41889)

```python
delegate_task(
    role="architect",   # resolves model/toolsets/skills/profile from config
    goal="Review docs/architecture/auth.md",
    context="...",
)
```

**3. Delegation guidance for parent agent** — built-in `agent-dispatch` skill or short SOUL.md template: "If task needs 3+ tool calls, specialist skill, or parallel work, prefer `delegate_task`. If short/conversational, handle inline." Fixes #48217 without hardcoding policy.

**4. Orchestration primitives** — minimal additions to `delegate_task`:
- `pipeline: [role_a, role_b, role_c]` — sequential, output flows to next
- `quality_gate: { role: "qa-lead", criteria: "...", max_retries: 2 }`
- `conflict_policy: "primary_wins" | "unanimous" | "report"` for parallel batches

**5. CLI surface**

```bash
hermes roles list / show / invoke / validate
```

---

## Non-Goals

- Not a workflow engine — Kanban exists for that.
- Not dynamic role discovery — #28767 is a separate scope.
- Not a replacement for `delegate_task` — this is a layer on top.
- Not ACP cross-vendor — #5257 is a different problem.

---

## Open Questions

1. **Config layout**: `~/.hermes/config.yaml` `agents.roles` block, or a dedicated `~/.hermes/roles/*.yaml` directory (each role its own file, more composable)?
2. **`role=` vs `profile=`**: merge into one parameter? `role=` is the user-facing name; profile is internal — a role may pin to one.
3. **Where does role resolution live**: extend `tools/delegate_tool.py`, or new `agent/role_resolver.py`?
4. **`hermes doctor` validation**: flag roles that reference missing models / profiles / skills?

---

## Related

#7517 (top-level multi-agent), #41889 (profile-backed delegate), #46880 (dual-model subagent), #35688 (background harness alt), #5876 (Council skill precedent), #28767 (self-evolving roles, downstream), #48217 (parent doesn't delegate), #44209 (event-sourced coordinator state), #5257 (ACP, orthogonal).

items.title: Multiplex mode: _apply_env_overrides reads API_SERVER_KEY from global os.environ, falsely enabling api_server for secondary profiles

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
### Description

When `gateway.multiplex_profiles` is enabled, `_apply_env_overrides()` in `gateway/config.py` reads `API_SERVER_KEY` and `API_SERVER_ENABLED` from `os.getenv()` — the **global process environment** — rather than from the profile-scoped secret store. This causes the gateway to falsely detect that a secondary profile has `api_server` enabled, aborting startup with a `MultiplexConfigError`.

### Root Cause

1. During module import, `gateway/run.py` loads the default profile's `.env` file into `os.environ` (including `API_SERVER_KEY`).
2. When `_start_one_profile_adapters()` runs for a secondary profile inside `_profile_runtime_scope()`, the scope sets up a profile-specific secret scope via `set_secret_scope()` — but does **not** clear the global `os.environ`.
3. `load_gateway_config()` → `_apply_env_overrides()` calls `os.getenv("API_SERVER_KEY")`, which finds the default profile's value still in the global environment.
4. The function then enables `api_server` for the secondary profile unconditionally.
5. The port-binding check in `_start_one_profile_adapters()` sees `api_server` enabled on a non-default profile and raises `MultiplexConfigError`.

### Impact

Multiplex mode is broken for any setup where the default profile's `.env` contains `API_SERVER_KEY` or `API_SERVER_ENABLED`. The error message points the user at the wrong fix (modify `config.yaml`), when the real issue is in env-var isolation.

### Affected Code

`gateway/config.py`, `_apply_env_overrides()`:

```python
api_server_enabled = os.getenv("API_SERVER_ENABLED", "").lower() in {"true", "1", "yes"}
api_server_key = os.getenv("API_SERVER_KEY", "")
...
if api_server_enabled or api_server_key:
    config.platforms[Platform.API_SERVER].enabled = True
```

Uses `os.getenv()` (global) instead of profile-scoped `get_secret()`.

### Suggested Fix

Change `_apply_env_overrides()` to read `API_SERVER_KEY` from the profile-scoped secret store (`get_secret()`) instead of `os.getenv()`.

### Workaround

Set `multiplex_profiles: false` in config.yaml.

### Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.17.0 (commit 0c3f197c)
- multiplex_profiles: true
- Secondary profile with no api_server in config.yaml

items.title: Desktop/TUI session view does not show messages arriving from gateway platforms

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Description

When the same Hermes session is used from both the Desktop GUI (TUI) and a gateway messaging platform (WeChat, Feishu, Telegram, etc.), messages that arrive from the gateway are stored in `state.db` correctly but are **not visible** in the Desktop GUI session view. The GUI only shows the messages that were loaded when the session was first opened, and never refreshes.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect Hermes Gateway to WeChat (or any messaging platform)
2. Start a conversation from WeChat phone
3. Open the same session in Desktop GUI (under WeChat section or Sessions section)
4. Continue the conversation by typing from the Desktop GUI
5. Send a message from WeChat phone -> Desktop GUI session view does NOT show it
6. Send another message from Desktop GUI -> also not visible from WeChat
7. Close and reopen the session in Desktop GUI -> all messages appear correctly

## Expected Behavior

The Desktop GUI session view should display ALL messages in the session regardless of source platform, and should refresh when new messages arrive from gateway sources.

## Actual Behavior

The Desktop GUI session view loads messages once via `get_messages_as_conversation()` in `tui_gateway/server.py` and caches them in memory without any polling or event-based update mechanism. Messages arriving from gateway platforms after the session is opened are stored in `state.db` but never displayed.

## Technical Root Cause

In `tui_gateway/server.py`, when a session is resumed (around line 4632):

```python
history = db.get_messages_as_conversation(target)
```

This is loaded once at session-open time and stored as:

```python
_sessions[sid] = {
    "history": history,
    ...
}
```

There is no mechanism (polling, WebSocket event, or periodic refresh) to update this cached history when new messages arrive from gateway platforms via `state.db`.

## Verification

Confirmed by inspecting `state.db` directly: all messages from both gateway and Desktop GUI exist in the same session. The data layer is correct; only the TUI display needs a refresh mechanism.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10
- Hermes Desktop GUI (Electron app)
- Gateway platforms affected: WeChat, Feishu (likely all platforms)

## Additional Context

This issue is most noticeable for users who switch between Desktop GUI and a messaging platform within the same conversation. The same behavior was confirmed on the Feishu integration as well.

The local terminal backend on Windows spawns bash.exe via subprocess.Popen() without the CREATE_NO_WINDOW (0x08000000) creation flag. Without this flag, Windows briefly creates a visible console window for the child process before it's redirected/hidden.

Likely location: the subprocess spawning code in the local terminal backend (e.g., environment executor or shell session manager). Adding creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NO_WINDOW when sys.platform == "win32" should fix it.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

import subprocess, sys

kwargs = {}
if sys.platform == "win32":
    kwargs["creationflags"] = subprocess.CREATE_NO_WINDOW

subprocess.Popen(["bash", "-c", command], **kwargs)

items.body:
## Problem

Hermes supports CLI and Gateway (Telegram, Discord, Slack, etc.) but they run as **completely separate sessions** — different context windows, different conversation histories.

If I start a complex debugging session in CLI, I can't continue that same conversation from Telegram when I step away from my desk. I have to re-explain everything from scratch.

## Use Case

1. Start a long debugging / build task on CLI (full terminal + file access)
2. Step away from desk
3. Check progress or give follow-up instructions from phone via Telegram
4. The assistant knows the full context — no cold start

## Current Architecture

- Each platform creates its own `state.db` entry with isolated messages
- No mechanism to share or attach context between CLI and Gateway sessions
- `/resume` only searches within the same platform/source type

## Proposed Solutions (open for discussion)

**Option A — Session Linking:**
- A session created on CLI can be "attached" to a Telegram chat (or vice versa)
- New messages from either side append to the *same* conversation
- Role alternation preserved cross-platform

**Option B — Context Forwarding:**
- A CLI session can "forward" its recent N messages (full or summarized) to a Gateway session
- The Gateway session picks up from that forwarded context

**Option C — Unified Session ID:**
- Allow binding a session to multiple `platform:chat_id` pairs at creation time
- Any bound platform can interact with the same session

## Why It Matters

Hermes' multi-platform gateway is a unique advantage over Claude Code / Codex / OpenCode. Making sessions portable across platforms would unlock the "your AI everywhere" vision — start on desktop, continue on mobile, check in from any chat platform.

I'm happy to help test or provide more details if this direction is interesting.

items.body:
## Telegram: outbound message stored as incoming in inbox (unread badge stuck)

### Environment
- Hermes version: **0.17.0** (update_check reports 72 commits behind)
- Platform: macOS 26.5.1, local install
- Channel: Telegram, single account, default home channel
- Hermes is the operator for `telegram` (1 connected platform)

### Summary
After upgrading from **0.16.x → 0.17.0**, every message Hermes **sends** to the user on Telegram shows up in the inbox/feed as if it were an **incoming unread** message. The unread badge stays incremented and never clears after reading on the Telegram client.

Result: the inbox unread count grows by one for every outbound message Hermes produces, including the empty/deliverability pings. On a long session this makes the inbox counter meaningless — it reflects "things I said" rather than "things you still need to read."

### Repro
1. Install Hermes 0.16.x, send a few outbound messages. Inbox badge updates only when the user messages Hermes. ✓
2. Upgrade to 0.17.0.
3. Have Hermes send a message to the user on Telegram.
4. Open Telegram. The message appears in the chat, **and** an unread indicator is raised on the user side for that message Hermes itself just sent.
5. Open and read the message in Telegram. Badge remains.
6. Send another message. Counter increments again.

### Expected
- Outbound messages from Hermes do **not** add to the inbox unread count.
- Unread badge tracks only inbound messages from the user, or unsynced outbound state — not the local echo of delivered sends.

### Actual
- Every outbound message increments the inbox unread count by 1.
- Counter persists after the user opens the message in Telegram.
- Inbox unread is effectively "outbound messages this session" instead of "inbound unread from user."

### Suspected cause (where I'd start looking)
There is a clear Telegram-touching change between v0.16 and v0.17 that lines up with the regression. My best guess is the inbox/feed now treats locally-echoed outbound messages as `from_user = "user"` (or omits the direction flag) when persisting, so the unread aggregator counts them as inbound. I'd start the bisect at the Telegram channel adapter in this release, not at the model or tool layer.

### Impact
- "What needs my attention" signal is lost — the badge reflects noise.
- Hard to tell if Hermes has an actual unread question waiting.
- For a solo operator on ADHD, this is a working-memory hit: I can't trust the counter to triage.

### Severity
Medium — not a data-loss bug, but it silently breaks a core "what's waiting" affordance and makes the inbox counter useless for triage.

### Extra context I can provide if useful
- Concrete inbox counter before/after a single outbound message.
- The Telegram chat IDs involved.
- The hermes-channel/telegram module file path and any relevant log lines from `~/.hermes/logs/`.

Happy to bisect a release tag and run a 0.16 vs 0.17 A/B if that helps narrow it faster.

items.title: [Bug]: `/learn` writes skill descriptions that exceed its own documented ≤60-char standard
items.body:
the `/learn` docs say the command authors skills to "house authoring standards (≤60-char description, the standard section order, Hermes-tool framing, no invented commands)" (user-guide → features → skills, section "Learning a skill from sources (`/learn`)": https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/skills). in practice the generated `description` runs well over 60 characters.

**Repro:** four `/learn` runs on Hermes Agent v0.17.0, measuring the `description` field length in the SKILL.md it wrote:

| run | description length |
|-----|-------------------|
| fallback-providers | 202 |
| disk-space | 123 |
| kill-process | 60 |
| cron-debug | 164 |

3 of 4 overshot, up to 202 chars against a documented ≤60 standard.

the real 202-char frontmatter it produced (author value redacted, see the separate author issue):

```yaml
---
name: hermes-fallback-providers
description: "Configure Hermes fallback_providers so calls fail over to an alternate provider+model on primary errors (HTTP 429, etc.). Covers the pin-both-provider-and-model gotcha and the hand-edit-config caveat."
version: 1.0.0
author: <auto-filled>
metadata:
  hermes:
    tags: [hermes, setup, configuration, providers, reliability]
---
```

**Why it matters:** the description is not cosmetic. the system-prompt skill index truncates descriptions to 60 chars (see #13944) and that line loads every session, so the index cuts an over-length description with no warning and the routing signal past char 60 never loads. `/learn` overshooting its own ≤60 standard degrades the thing that standard exists to protect.

**Where it looks to come from:** skill creation validates the description only against `MAX_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH = 1024` (`tools/skills_tool.py`); the ≤60 house standard is documented but is not passed to or enforced at generation time, so the model writes a full sentence. the skill *content* `/learn` produces is good; it is the frontmatter that overshoots.

**Suggested fix:** have `/learn` target ≤60 for the generated `description` (align the generation prompt with the documented standard, and warn or trim on overshoot), so the index line is not truncated.

related, not duplicates: #13944 (index truncates to 60), #46024 (make the truncation limit configurable). those address the index side; this is `/learn` not meeting its own documented generation standard.

_(reproduced across 4 `/learn` runs on Hermes Agent v0.17.0.)_

items.title: [Bug]: `/learn` auto-fills the skill `author` field with the host OS username (no opt-in, privacy leak)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
`/learn` populates the `author` frontmatter field on its own, and it defaults to the machine's OS username. the docs say nothing about the `author` field, so it happens with no warning.

**Repro:** four `/learn` runs on Hermes Agent v0.17.0. the `author` value resolved to the host's OS user in 3 of 4 runs, and to a different identity once, so it is also inconsistent run to run on the same machine.

**Why it matters:** skills are meant to be shared. they get committed to repos and pushed to the skills hub. when `author` is auto-filled from the OS account, that personal username (often a real name) ships inside the published SKILL.md without the user ever choosing to put it there. it is a privacy leak the user did not opt into, and nothing in the `/learn` flow or the docs surfaces it.

**Where it looks to come from:** skill creation (`tools/skill_manager_tool.py`) sets no `author` and gives the model no author guidance. separately, the agent's environment context surfaces the OS username: the backend probe in `agent/prompt_builder.py` emits `user=$(whoami …)` into the system prompt as an environment hint. so when the model writes the frontmatter it fills `author` from the most salient identity available, which is that OS username. when a stronger identity is present in context it uses that instead, which is why the value varies.

**Suggested fix:** do not auto-fill `author` from the OS user. either omit the field or use a configured display name (a `hermes config` value); never fall back to the raw OS account name.

dedup: no existing issue covers author auto-fill; nearest is #42786 (mismatched dir/frontmatter name on bundled skills), which is a different problem.

_(reproduced across 4 `/learn` runs on Hermes Agent v0.17.0. the OS username is redacted here.)_

items.title: Slack: add send_clarify with Block Kit interactive buttons
items.body:
## Problem

The Slack adapter does not override `send_clarify()`, so when the `clarify` tool fires on Slack, it falls back to the base adapter's numbered-text implementation. This produces a raw JSON/code-block rendering instead of an interactive prompt:

- No clickable buttons — the user cannot select an option
- The text-capture fallback (`mark_awaiting_text`) is unreliable on Slack
- Raw tool-call JSON leaks into the chat instead of a formatted question

## Expected behavior

The Slack adapter should render `clarify` prompts using Block Kit interactive buttons, matching the pattern already used for approval prompts (`send_exec_approval`) and slash-confirm prompts.

## Implementation sketch

Three additions to `gateway/platforms/slack.py`:

1. **`send_clarify` method** — Build a Block Kit message with:
   - A section block containing the question text
   - An actions block with one button per choice (action_id: `hermes_clarify_choice`, value: `{clarify_id}::{idx}::{choice_text}`)
   - An "Other..." button (action_id: `hermes_clarify_other`, value: `{clarify_id}`) that calls `mark_awaiting_text()` for free-text capture
   - Falls back to plain text if Block Kit fails

2. **`_handle_clarify_action` callback** — Handle button clicks:
   - `hermes_clarify_choice`: Extract choice from value, update message to show selection, call `resolve_gateway_clarify()`
   - `hermes_clarify_other`: Call `mark_awaiting_text()`, update message to show "Type your answer below"

3. **Handler registration** — Register both action IDs via `self._app.action()` alongside existing approval/confirm handlers

## Reference

The approval prompt at `_handle_approval_action` / `send_exec_approval` follows the exact same Block Kit button pattern and can serve as a template.

items.body:
a user running Hermes on Railway reports Hermes keeps generating files until the disk fills with "no space left on device", at which point Hermes stops. they asked whether others have seen it.

- source: https://www.reddit.com/r/hermesagent/comments/1uew23a/infinitive_generation_of_log_file_bug/

**Why this is worth prioritising:** it is an availability and data-loss failure. once the disk is full the agent cannot write state or logs and the whole instance goes down, and on a hosted container the user cannot easily clear space to recover.

**What I checked (so the issue points the right way):** the app log files are not the cause. `hermes_logging.py` writes them through a `RotatingFileHandler`, and on my own 24/7 instance the log directory is bounded: ~40MB total, each file capped near 5MB. so rotated logs are working. the disk-fill is coming from elsewhere, and there are two likely sources:

1. **artifact directories with no default retention.** on my instance, the directories that grow without bound are `state-snapshots` (~750MB) and per-run cron output (`cron/output/<job>/`, one file per run, ~1,500 files), plus the browser profile. none of these self-prune. my instance only stays healthy because I run a cleanup job and the bundled disk-cleanup plugin; a fresh or hosted deploy without those keeps accumulating until the volume is full.
2. **stdout/stderr is not size-bounded.** the rotating handlers cover Hermes' own log files, but the stream handler that writes to stdout is not rotated. if the deploy or a supervisor captures stdout to a file (common on hosted platforms), that capture grows unbounded regardless of the log rotation.

**Most useful next steps:**
1. from the reporter: run `du -sh ~/.hermes/*/` and report which directory is filling the disk, the Hermes version, the Railway disk size, whether the disk-cleanup plugin or any cleanup cron is enabled, and whether the platform captures stdout to a file.
2. depending on the answer: ship sane default retention for `state-snapshots` and `cron/output`, make disk-cleanup discoverable or default-on for hosted deploys, and document that stdout is not size-bounded.

possibly related, not duplicates: the bundled disk-cleanup plugin (`plugins/disk-cleanup`); #41683 (preflight writable runtime paths for history/logs/pastes).

items.title: [Bug]: Slack mention detection (allow_bots=mentions, is_mentioned, require_mention) only inspects flat top-level text, so @mentions present only in Block Kit blocks are silently dropped
items.body:
## Version

`v2026.6.19` (line numbers below are from this tag; the logic appears unchanged on `main`).

## Summary

When another Slack app posts a message that **@mentions the Hermes bot**, but builds the message with **Block Kit `blocks`** (e.g. a `rich_text` section containing a `user` element) and only a plain fallback string in the top-level `text` field, Hermes **silently drops the message** under `slack.allow_bots: mentions`.

The same blind spot affects the normal mention router (`is_mentioned` / `require_mention` / `strict_mention`): the mention is invisible there too, because both checks read only the flat `text` field — not the text that `_extract_text_from_slack_blocks()` would recover from the blocks.

Net effect: there is **no configuration** that lets a bot's Block-Kit-only mention reach the agent while still gating on mentions. The only workarounds are to disable mention gating entirely (process *all* messages in the channel) or to change the *sending* app to embed the `<@UID>` in the flat `text`.

## Reproduction

1. Run the Slack gateway with:
   ```yaml
   slack:
     require_mention: true
     strict_mention: true
     allow_bots: mentions
   ```
2. Invite the Hermes bot to a channel.
3. From a **second Slack app**, post a message into that channel that mentions the Hermes bot, constructed via the Block Kit `blocks` array, e.g.:
   ```json
   {
     "text": "Release notification",
     "blocks": [
       {
         "type": "rich_text",
         "elements": [
           {
             "type": "rich_text_section",
             "elements": [
               { "type": "text", "text": "Hey " },
               { "type": "user", "user_id": "U_HERMES_BOT" },
               { "type": "text", "text": "! I will do a release" }
             ]
           }
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
   ```
   Note the top-level `text` ("Release notification") does **not** contain `<@U_HERMES_BOT>`; the mention lives only in `blocks`.

### Expected

Because the message genuinely @mentions the bot, `allow_bots: mentions` should accept it and the agent should be triggered (subject to the normal mention rules).

### Actual

The message is silently dropped — no log line, no trace. Verified against the Slack API: such messages have the mention only in `blocks`, never in the flat `text`:

```
text_has_mention(<@U_HERMES_BOT> in event.text)         -> false
blocks_has_mention(user_id present in event.blocks)     -> true
```

## Root cause

Two independent gates both read only the flat top-level `text`, and the block-text recovery happens *after* the first gate has already `return`ed.

**1. Bot-message filter** — `gateway/platforms/slack.py` (~L2267):

```python
if event.get("bot_id") or event.get("subtype") == "bot_message":
    allow_bots = self.config.extra.get("allow_bots", "")
    if not allow_bots:
        allow_bots = os.getenv("SLACK_ALLOW_BOTS", "none")
    allow_bots = str(allow_bots).lower().strip()
    if allow_bots == "none":
        return
    elif allow_bots == "mentions":
        text_check = event.get("text", "")          # <-- flat text only
        if self._bot_user_id and f"<@{self._bot_user_id}>" not in text_check:
            return                                    # <-- silent drop
```

**2. Block text is only merged *later*** — `gateway/platforms/slack.py` (~L2316), i.e. after the bot filter has already returned:

```python
text = original_text
blocks = event.get("blocks")
if blocks:
    blocks_text = _extract_text_from_slack_blocks(blocks)   # renders user elems as <@UID>
    ...
    text = (text.strip() + "\n" + stripped_blocks).strip()
```

`_extract_text_from_slack_blocks()` already converts a `user` rich-text element into `<@{user_id}>` — so the mention *is* recoverable; it is just never consulted by the gate.

**3. The normal mention router has the same bug** — `gateway/platforms/slack.py` (~L2485):

```python
routing_text = original_text or ""                  # <-- flat text, NOT the merged text
is_mentioned = bot_uid and f"<@{bot_uid}>" in routing_text
```

So even with `allow_bots: all`, a Block-Kit-only mention yields `is_mentioned == false`, and the message is then dropped by `strict_mention` (`strict and not is_mentioned -> return`) or by the `require_mention` branch.

## Impact

- Apps that post via Block Kit (which is the default for any non-trivial formatted message, and what the modern composer / many bots emit) can mention Hermes and be ignored, with no diagnostics.
- `allow_bots: mentions` is effectively non-functional for Block-Kit senders.
- The only escape hatches are lossy: `require_mention: false` / `free_response_channels` (process *everything* in the channel), or modifying the upstream sender. `allow_bots` is global, so relaxing it widens exposure across every channel the bot is in.
- Failure is **silent** — no log on drop — which makes this very hard to diagnose in the field.

## Suggested fix

Compute mention detection from the **block-extracted text**, not the raw flat `text`, at both gates:

1. In the bot-message filter, build the `text_check` from `event.get("text", "")` **plus** `_extract_text_from_slack_blocks(event.get("blocks"))` before testing for `<@bot_user_id>`.
2. Set `routing_text` (for `is_mentioned`) from the same merged text rather than `original_text`.

Factoring the "flat text + block-extracted text" merge into a small helper used by both the bot filter and the router would keep them consistent.

Optionally: emit a `logger.debug` (or `info`) line when a bot message is dropped by the `mentions`/`strict`/`require` gates, so silent drops become diagnosable.

## Related

- #50732 — `slack.mention_patterns` documented but silently ignored (different field; closed).
- #30091 — bot-to-bot messages dropped with `allow_bots=all` (different root cause: event-subscription gap; does not cover the blocks-vs-text mention gap).

items.title: Bug: unresolvable model silently persists hardcoded placeholder into sticky session binding → permanent 404 that survives config fixes & restarts

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

When `config.yaml`'s `model.default` cannot be resolved (e.g. `provider: custom` configured but `base_url`/`api_key` missing, or no model selected at all), `tui_gateway/server.py:_resolve_model()` returns a hardcoded placeholder `"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4"`. That placeholder is **persisted into the sticky `sessions.model` binding** via `create_session`, so the affected session **permanently 404s** (`Model not found`) on any endpoint that doesn't serve that model — and keeps 404-ing **even after the config is fixed and the process restarted**, because the session-level model binding wins over `config.yaml` on resume.

In short: a transient/config model-resolution failure is silently turned into a **persistent, sticky, self-healing-proof session failure**.

## Reproduce

`config.yaml` (provider set, but unresolvable model — e.g. missing/empty `model.default`):

```yaml
model:
  provider: custom
  base_url: https://my-gateway.example/v1
  api_key: <key>
  # default:  ← intentionally absent
```

1. Start the dashboard, open a chat → a new session row is created.
2. The `sessions.model` column for that row is written as `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4` (the hardcoded fallback).
3. The endpoint returns `HTTP 404: Model not found: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4` on every turn.
4. **Fix the config** (set `model.default: <real-model>`) and **restart the process**.
5. Resume the session from step 1 → it **still 404s**, because the sticky `sessions.model` binding (`anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`) takes precedence over the corrected `config.yaml`.

## Root cause

`tui_gateway/server.py` (v0.17.0, commit `7fb2027d`):

```python
# line ~1667
def _resolve_model() -> str:
    env = (os.environ.get("HERMES_MODEL", "") or os.environ.get("HERMES_INFERENCE_MODEL", "")).strip()
    if env:
        return env
    m = _load_cfg().get("model", "")
    if isinstance(m, dict):
        return str(m.get("default", "") or "").strip()
    if isinstance(m, str) and m:
        return m.strip()
    return "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4"   # ← hardcoded placeholder
```

This placeholder flows into two persistence sites:

```python
# line ~1411  (desktop session row)
db.create_session(key, source=..., model=row_model, ...)          # row_model falls back to _resolve_model()

# line ~6506  (TUI /branch)
db.create_session(new_key, source=..., model=_resolve_model(), ...)
```

`gateway/run.py:_resolve_gateway_model` (the per-turn resolver) already does the right thing — it returns `""` on failure:

```python
# line ~2188
def _resolve_gateway_model(config=None) -> str:
    ...
    return model_cfg.get("default") or model_cfg.get("model") or ""   # empty on failure
```

…but that empty contract is defeated at session-creation time, because `tui_gateway` writes the placeholder into `sessions.model` first, and on resume the session-level binding short-circuits the per-turn resolver (gateway/run.py ~3330: `model = _resolve_gateway_model(user_config)` is only consulted when there is **no** session override).

Two compounding problems:

1. **The placeholder is a guaranteed-404 value** on most custom/OpenAI-compatible endpoints (the model simply isn't there). It's also **inconsistent** with the rest of the codebase, which defaults to the `4.6` variant (`gateway/run.py:9157`, `run_agent.py:5371`, `hermes_cli/models.py`).
2. **The placeholder is persisted** into a binding that is *sticky* and *highest-priority*, so the failure outlives its own cause.

## Expected behavior

- Resolution failure should **not** silently pick a concrete model name that the user never chose. Either fail loudly (so the user fixes their config), or return empty and let the per-turn resolver re-read `config.yaml` on each turn.
- A model name that was never explicitly selected by the user should **not** be written into the sticky `sessions.model` binding.

## Suggested fix

Minimal, mirrors the existing `_resolve_gateway_model` contract:

```python
def _resolve_model() -> str:
    ...
    return ""   # was: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4"
```

and coerce empty → `None` at the two `create_session` call sites so no placeholder is persisted:

```python
# ~1411
model=row_model or None,
# ~6506
model=(_resolve_model() or None),
```

With this, an empty `sessions.model` row lets the per-turn resolver re-read `config.yaml` on resume — so once the config is fixed, existing sessions self-heal on the next turn instead of 404-ing forever.

## Environment

- hermes-agent `0.17.0` (commit `7fb2027d`)
- Provider: custom (OpenAI-compatible gateway); reproduces on any endpoint that doesn't serve `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`

## Workaround

Manually rewrite the affected rows: `UPDATE sessions SET model = '<real-model>' WHERE model = 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4';` in `state.db` (per `HERMES_HOME`), then restart the dashboard process.

## Impact

Medium. Requires a config/resolution failure as a precondition, but once hit the failure is **silent** (user just sees dead/erroring chat) and **persists across config fixes and restarts** — which is the part that makes it a real footgun rather than a transient blip.

items.body: ## Bug Description The verify-on-stop guard added in #52296 ("Add verification stop loop") and #52297 ("Support ad-hoc verification scripts") leaks internal verification machinery into user-facing replies on messaging surfaces (Telegram, Discord, etc.). When an agent bound to a Telegram topic edits local files in a workspace that has project facts but no canonical test command, the harness injects the edit -> verify nudge (`agent/verification_stop.py` `build_verify_on_stop_nudge`). With no suite detected, the nudge instructs the model to write a `/tmp/hermes-verify-*.py` script, run it, and "summarize it explicitly as ad-hoc verification rather than suite green." The model complies, and that ad-hoc verification summary becomes the final turn response, which the gateway delivers verbatim to the end user as chat noise. The guard is valuable for a coding CLI session. On a chat surface the verification receipt is internal machinery the human user should never see. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Run an agent bound to a Telegram (or Discord) topic via the gateway. 2. Have it edit one or more local files in a directory that resolves project facts (`agent/coding_context.project_facts_for`) but has no canonical `verifyCommands` (for example a shell script + a `CLAUDE.md`, no test runner). 3. Let the turn finish. 4. The agent's reply to the chat is the ad-hoc verification receipt rather than (or appended to) a normal answer. ## Expected vs Actual - Expected: on a messaging surface, the user receives the normal answer; verification, if it runs, stays internal. - Actual: the user receives an internal verification receipt, for example: ``` Ad-hoc verification rerun for the changed files. Temporary script: /tmp/hermes-verify-4hupyoi1.py Result: PASS changed_files=3 checks=deploy helper new-route coverage, CLAUDE allowlist/exclusion guardrails, ... cleanup=removed Verified: - convertx-static-deploy.sh includes all four new high-volume routes ... - CLAUDE.md includes the new route allowlist ... This is ad-hoc verification, not a canonical full suite green. ``` A screenshot of the leak in a live Telegram topic is attached in a comment below. ## Root Cause `verify_on_stop_enabled()` (`agent/verification_stop.py`) defaults to `True` for every session, and the call site `agent/conversation_loop.py:4538` passes no delivery-surface context. So a gateway messaging session gets the same edit -> verify -> narrate behavior as a coding CLI session, and the post-nudge verification summary is delivered to the chat user. The signal to distinguish surfaces already exists: the gateway binds the platform value (for example `telegram`) to `HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM` (`gateway/run.py` `_set_session_env`), and CLI/TUI set `HERMES_SESSION_SOURCE`. Sibling code in `agent/skill_commands.py` and `agent/prompt_builder.py` already reads `HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM` for per-platform behavior. ## Proposed Fix Make the verify-on-stop default surface-aware: keep it ON for interactive coding surfaces (CLI, TUI, desktop) and programmatic callers, and default it OFF on conversational messaging surfaces, with an explicit `HERMES_VERIFY_ON_STOP` env var or a boolean `agent.verify_on_stop` config still overriding in either direction. A PR implementing this is linked below. ## Environment - Affects current `main` (the originating PRs #52296 / #52297 merged 2026-06-25). - Surface: gateway messaging platforms (Telegram confirmed; Discord, Slack, Signal, WhatsApp, etc. share the path).
